category: military expedition (described by participants as a pilgrimage)
location: From Clermont (Auvergne) across Europe, Constantinople, and Anatolia to Antioch and Jerusalem

date.note: Pope Urban II preached the expedition at the Council of Clermont on 27 November 1095, after Byzantine envoys of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos had appealed for military help at the papal council of Piacenza in March 1095. The main armies left in 1096, took Nicaea and won at Dorylaeum in 1097, captured Antioch in June 1098, and stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 by the date given in the Latin accounts; Ibn al-Qalanisi dates the surrender of what Gibb's translation renders as 'the sanctuary [of David]' (which Gibb, p. 45 n. 1, identifies as the Citadel of Jerusalem, the Tower of David) to 22 Sha'ban 492, which Gibb converts to 14 July 1099. The campaign ended with the defeat of a Fatimid army near Ascalon in August 1099.

summary: The First Crusade was the armed expedition from Latin Europe proclaimed by Pope Urban II at Clermont in November 1095, which crossed Byzantine territory and Anatolia, captured Antioch in 1098, and took Jerusalem from its Fatimid garrison in July 1099, followed by a massacre of many of the city's inhabitants. It led to the founding of Latin states in Syria and Palestine; its motives, its name, and the scale of the killing in Jerusalem are debated by historians.
description:
In March 1095 envoys of the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos asked Pope Urban II for military help against the Seljuk Turks, who had taken much of Anatolia after the battle of Manzikert (1071). On 27 November 1095, at the close of a reforming council at Clermont, Urban preached an armed expedition to the East. No authentic text of the sermon survives: the versions of Fulcher of Chartres, Robert the Monk, Baldric of Dol, and Guibert of Nogent, and the shorter account of the Gesta Francorum, were written afterwards, several of them after the capture of Jerusalem, and they differ. In Fulcher's version Urban urges his hearers to help 'your brethren who live in the east', who 'are in urgent need of your help', and promises that 'all who die by the way, whether by land or by sea, or in battle against the pagans, shall have immediate remission of sins', but this version does not name Jerusalem; Urban's own letter of instruction of December 1095 speaks of an enemy that had 'laid waste the churches of God in the regions of the Orient' and held 'the Holy City of Christ' in servitude, and other versions of the sermon, several written after 1099, give Jerusalem a central place. Historians debate how central the liberation of Jerusalem was to Urban's original aim, as against military aid to Byzantium. The participants called themselves pilgrims (peregrini) and their undertaking a journey (iter) to Jerusalem; the vocabulary of 'crusade' (crucesignati, cruciata) came into general use only later.

The first contingents, popular bands associated with preachers such as Peter the Hermit, set out in the spring of 1096; some of them attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland on their way east, and most were destroyed in Anatolia in October 1096. The princely armies, led among others by Godfrey of Bouillon, Raymond of Saint-Gilles (count of Toulouse), Bohemond of Taranto, Robert of Normandy, and Robert of Flanders, assembled at Constantinople in 1096-1097, where most leaders swore oaths to Alexios. They took Nicaea (handed over to the Byzantines in June 1097), defeated a Seljuk army at Dorylaeum (July 1097), besieged Antioch from October 1097, entered it in June 1098, and then defeated the relief army of Kerbogha of Mosul. Baldwin of Boulogne meanwhile took control of Edessa. The Muslim Near East was politically divided: the Great Seljuk sultanate had fragmented after the death of Malik-Shah in 1092, the Seljuk rulers of Aleppo and Damascus were rivals, and Fatimid Egypt had taken Jerusalem from Turkish control in 1098. Ibn al-Qalanisi of Damascus records that at Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in December 1098 the Franks captured the town and, 'after promising them safety, dealt treacherously with them'.

The crusaders reached Jerusalem in June 1099 and stormed it in mid-July. The Latin participants themselves describe a massacre. The anonymous Gesta Francorum says that 'the slaughter was so great that our men waded in blood up to their ankles' as far as the 'Temple of Solomon' (Templum Salomonis, the Latin name for the Aqsa mosque on the Haram al-Sharif); Raymond of Aguilers writes that 'in the Temple and porch of Solomon, men rode in blood up to their knees and bridle reins', and calls it 'a just and splendid judgment of God', a theological verdict reported here as his own; Fulcher of Chartres states that 'in this temple almost ten thousand were killed'. In the Damascene chronicle of Ibn al-Qalanisi, as translated by Gibb, 'a number of the townsfolk fled to the sanctuary [of David], and a great host were killed. The Jews assembled in the synagogue, and the Franks burned it over their heads. The sanctuary was surrendered to them on guarantee of safety'; the bracketed gloss is Gibb's, and the 'sanctuary of David' is the place which Gibb (p. 45 n. 1) identifies as the Citadel of Jerusalem (the Tower of David), whose Fatimid garrison surrendered on terms, not the Haram. The Jewish experience of the conquest is also attested in Hebrew letters from the Cairo Geniza published by S. D. Goitein, among them a letter of the Karaite elders of Ascalon, which describe Jewish captives from Jerusalem, some killed and others ransomed together with books and Torah scrolls by Jewish communities with funds raised in Egypt. Ibn al-Athir, writing more than a century later at Mosul, reports that the Franks killed more than 70,000 people in the Aqsa mosque, among them many scholars and ascetics. Modern historians treat all such figures with caution, and the scale of the killing is debated: Benjamin Kedar, surveying the Latin and Arabic sources and their later historiography, concluded that the massacre in Jerusalem was considerably more extensive than in other captured towns, while Konrad Hirschler, studying the Arabic historiography, accepts that a massacre took place but argues that the earliest Egyptian and Syrian reports do not indicate one larger than at other towns, and that Ibn al-Athir's version, which became the standard Islamic narrative, reflects later elaboration.

After the capture Godfrey of Bouillon was chosen as ruler of Jerusalem, and in August 1099 the crusaders defeated a Fatimid army near Ascalon; Ibn al-Qalanisi reports about ten thousand killed there. Most surviving crusaders then returned home. The expedition left behind the county of Edessa, the principality of Antioch, which Bohemond kept for himself (Alexios and Byzantine writers treated this as a breach of the oath to restore former imperial cities to the emperor, while Bohemond's partisans held that Alexios's failure to come to Antioch in 1098 had released the crusaders from it; the dispute became a lasting grievance in Byzantine-Latin relations), and the kingdom of Jerusalem, later joined by the county of Tripoli. Historians debate why so many joined: Jonathan Riley-Smith, drawing on charters of departing crusaders, argued that the expedition was understood above all as a penitential act of devotion, against an older interpretation that explained recruitment chiefly by material motives such as land hunger, and other historians stress a mixture of religious, social, and political motives. The Byzantine view is preserved in the Alexiad of Anna Komnene, Alexios's daughter, written in the 1140s, which presents the arrival of the western armies as an alarming mass movement and Bohemond as an ambitious adversary of the empire; Jonathan Harris studies the expedition from the side of Byzantine policy. Historians also debate the name: Christopher Tyerman has argued that crusading took shape as a defined institution only in the later twelfth century, so that calling the expedition of 1095-1099 a 'crusade' is partly retrospective, while Riley-Smith treats it as the event in which the idea of crusading was formed. On the Muslim side, Carole Hillenbrand describes an initially fragmented response that developed over the twelfth century into a renewed ideology of jihad, in which the recovery of Jerusalem became central under Nur al-Din and Saladin.
editorial_notes: This entry is filed under christianity as a storage convention per ADR-0010, because the crusade was a Latin Christian undertaking, proclaimed by the pope and preached as a penitential undertaking; the filing is not a claim that the event belongs to one tradition. The Byzantine, Muslim, and Jewish dimensions are linked by relations and sourced in their own voices: Anna Komnene's Alexiad and Harris for the Byzantine side, the Arabic chronicles of Ibn al-Qalanisi and Ibn al-Athir and scholarship on the Islamic perspective (Hillenbrand, Hirschler) for the Muslim side, the Geniza letters published by Goitein for the Jews of Jerusalem in 1099, and, for the Jewish communities attacked in 1096, the Hebrew chronicles, through the relation to rhineland-massacres-1096 (neutrality principles #10 and #11). NEUTRALITY: the massacre in Jerusalem is described in the words of the participants and of the Muslim chroniclers; every casualty figure is attributed to the author who gives it, and none is adopted as correct (neutrality #2). Raymond of Aguilers' description of the killing as God's judgment is quoted as his attributed view, never adopted in editorial voice. Urban II's aims are given only as the sources state them, and the centrality of Jerusalem to his original plan is presented as debated. The dispute over Antioch is presented with both the Byzantine charge of oath-breaking and the counter-position of Bohemond's partisans, without adjudication. The Kedar-Hirschler disagreement over the scale of the massacre, the religious-versus-material debate over motives, and the debate over whether 'crusade' is an anachronistic name for the expedition of 1095-1099 are each presented as competing scholarly framings without adjudication. The vocabulary of each source ('pagans', 'Franks') is quoted as that source's language. SOURCING: the Latin primary lens is the Urban II sermon versions and Urban's letter, and the eyewitness accounts of the capture of Jerusalem (Gesta Francorum, Raymond of Aguilers, Fulcher of Chartres) in the public-domain translations of Thatcher and McNeal (1905), Duncan and Krey (1912), and Krey (1921), read directly on the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, so rated high for the quoted passages. The Arabic primary lens is Ibn al-Qalanisi in Gibb's translation, pp. 46-49 read directly from a scan of the printed pages (rated high for the quoted passages; Gibb's bracketed gloss 'the sanctuary [of David]' is kept so that the passage is not read as referring to the Haram), and Ibn al-Athir in D. S. Richards' translation (rated medium, the 70,000 figure not checked against the page). The Byzantine primary lens is Anna Komnene's Alexiad (Sewter's translation revised by Frankopan), and the Jewish lens on 1099 is Goitein's edition of the Geniza letters; both are rated medium, verified through publisher and bibliographic records, not read line-by-line. The outside-scholarship lens is Riley-Smith, Tyerman, and Asbridge on the Latin side, Harris on the Byzantine side, and Hillenbrand, Kedar, and Hirschler on the casualty question and the Islamic perspective; these were verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher pages, institutional repositories, and catalog records, and for Hirschler the published abstract was read, but their relevant passages were not read line-by-line, so they are rated medium. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited. Dates are given in CE with the hijri date where an Arabic source supplies it; the one-day difference between the Latin date (15 July) and Gibb's conversion of Ibn al-Qalanisi's date for the sanctuary's surrender (14 July) is recorded rather than resolved.

relations.note: In the spring and early summer of 1096 bands setting out on the expedition preached at Clermont attacked the Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms, Mainz, Cologne, and other Rhineland towns, the first large-scale violence associated with the crusade.
The participants understood the expedition as a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and called themselves pilgrims (peregrini); historians describe the First Crusade as an armed pilgrimage.

In the versions of Urban II's preaching, participation carried spiritual benefits described as the remission of sins or as a substitute for penance, a grant that historians treat as an antecedent of the later crusade indulgence.
The expedition was proclaimed by Pope Urban II at a council of the reform papacy, and the papal call to arms became a defining feature of later crusades.

The First Crusade was proclaimed by Pope Urban II and undertaken as a penitential armed pilgrimage under the authority of the Latin church, beginning the crusading movement of medieval Latin Christianity.

The expedition followed an appeal for help from the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos and passed through Constantinople, where most leaders swore oaths to him; disputes over those oaths, especially over Antioch, strained relations between the Latin and Greek Christian worlds.

The expedition took place four decades after the mutual excommunications of 1054; its passage through Byzantine territory and the later Latin control of Antioch belong to the history of Latin-Greek relations that the schism describes.
Bernard of Clairvaux preached the Second Crusade (1146-1147), launched after the fall of Edessa, one of the states founded during the First Crusade.
The Fourth Crusade, a later expedition in the movement begun in 1095, was diverted to Constantinople and sacked it in 1204.

sources.citation: Urban II's sermon at Clermont (1095) in the versions of Fulcher of Chartres, Robert the Monk, the Gesta Francorum, Baldric of Dol, and Guibert of Nogent, with Urban II's letter of instruction (December 1095), trans. Oliver J. Thatcher and Edgar Holmes McNeal, A Source Book for Medieval History (New York: Scribner's, 1905), Dana C. Munro (1895), and August C. Krey, The First Crusade: The Accounts of Eyewitnesses and Participants (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1921); presented together on the Internet Medieval Sourcebook (Fordham University). The Latin primary lens on the proclamation. Read directly; the quoted passages from Fulcher's version ('your brethren who live in the east are in urgent need of your help'; 'All who die by the way, whether by land or by sea, or in battle against the pagans, shall have immediate remission of sins') were verified against the text.

sources.citation: Ibn al-Qalanisi. The Damascus Chronicle of the Crusades: Extracted and Translated from the Chronicle of Ibn al-Qalanisi, trans. H. A. R. Gibb. London: Luzac, 1932 (reprinted Mineola, NY: Dover, 2002), 46-49. The near-contemporary Damascene chronicle (Dhayl ta'rikh Dimashq) covering 1097-1159; the Arabic primary lens. Pages 46-49 (years 491-492 AH) were read directly from a scan of the printed pages; quoted passages verified: Ma'arrat al-Nu'man ('after promising them safety, dealt treacherously with them'), Jerusalem ('a great host were killed. The Jews assembled in the synagogue, and the Franks burned it over their heads'; the sanctuary 'surrendered to them on guarantee of safety on the 22nd of Sha'ban (14th July)'), and Ascalon ('about ten thousand souls').
sources.license: Translation published 1932; read from a scan of pp. 46-49 for the quoted passages. Underlying Arabic text public domain.

Crusade Texts in Translation 13. Aldershot: Ashgate, 2006. The Mosul historian's universal chronicle, written in the early thirteenth century, cited for its account of the capture of Jerusalem and the figure of more than 70,000 killed in the Aqsa mosque; the later Arabic primary lens. Peer-reviewed study of the sources for the massacre and of its treatment in Western historiography from the twelfth century to the present, concluding that the massacre in Jerusalem was considerably more extensive than in other towns; one side of the scholarly debate on its scale.
